episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! transcript_window.text: My phone's over there.
All right, let's move on.
So question number three.
I struggled with this one.
I'm curious If you could time travel back and develop this thing yourself, if we're putting you next to George, you're building this thing together, could you make the product more successful?
And I want to talk in particular about the very first ones.
Is there anything you would have changed?
I came up empty on this one that I think, and this might be to your point, Richard, why it's right place, right time.
That I'm not sure I could have made it cheaper or pushed in any particular direction or made sure to add a feature or something.
I don't know.
I'm curious if either of you have any ideas.
I do think they should have kept a remote, is it?
Oh, that's a good one.
I just, I feel like it became, and this to our conversation about the phone, it became something that only the person with the phone had control of.
You know, in a home, I had young children at the time.
And the original idea had been to create a physical remote for products.
So I don't think it would have hurt to have kept the remote in there.
I don't think that would have made it more successful, though.
I think it just would have helped with that one flaw.
Richard, what about you?
Any ideas?
Yeah, two things.
I agree completely with the remote idea.
Personally, I don't really like most of the remote or controller options they've come out with.
The first one, the tap, which I really prefer to call the press really hard because it's kinetically powered.
So you really have to press on it to generate the power to send the signal.
